newsitem.title: USA: Blue chips dragged lower by weak technology shares.
newsitem.headline: Blue chips dragged lower by weak technology shares.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks closed lower Monday as a sharp drop in technology shares ended a rally sparked by news of Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp.'s mega-merger.

The Dow Jones industrial average ended down 36.52 points at 6,268.35 after a drop of more than 50 points activated the New York Stock Exchange's limits on programme trading. In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 1,654 to 874 on active volume of 447 million shares on the NYSE.
The technology-laden Nasdaq Composite index plunged 23.93 points to 1,260.98, its steepest fall since July 23.
Analysts said profit-taking in technology stocks snowballed after computer and electronics retailer Circuit City Stores Inc. reported disappointing earnings.

The market was extremely volatile, as investors bid up blue-chip stocks from the opening on Boeing's blockbuster $13.3 billion acquisition of McDonnell Douglas. Boeing rose 4 to 100-3/4 and McDonnell Douglas jumped 10-1/2 to 62-1/2.
Technology shares also joined in the rally.

The mood of investors soured in afternoon trading on news that Circuit City's quarterly earnings slumped to $19.8 million from $31.5 million a year ago. The Richmond, Va.-based company cited soft personal computer sales for the drop.
Analysts said the already apprehensive market seized on the Circuit City news and took the opportunity to sell.

"The market is assuming that because one bad retailer reported sloppy earnings, the entire tech industry is going to hell in a handbasket," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management. "Technology investors tend to be very nervous and in this case the response was overblown."
Some of the session's biggest losses were posted by brand-name technology stocks, which analysts saw as a sign investors had decided to take some of their profits.
"If you're going to take profits in this market, the large-cap techs would clearly be the obvious targets," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp.
International Business Machines Corp. fell 4-1/8 to 148-3/4 and Intel Corp. lost 5-1/8 to 127-1/4. Microsoft Corp. fell 3-1/4 to 76-3/4.
Heightened caution was also evident when Morgan Stanley's global strategist, Barton Biggs recommended shifting some money out of stocks into cash and bonds.

The move altered Morgan Stanley's global asset allocation portfolio to 56 percent stocks, 29 percent bonds and 15 percent cash. The portfolio had been weighted 74 percent to stocks and 26 percent to bonds before the switch.
Wall Street was also cautious ahead of Tuesday's meeting of the Federal Reserve's interest-rate setting Federal Open Market Committtee.
Release of stronger-than-expected industrial production data depressed the bond market, a response analysts attributed to the proximity of the Fed meeting.
Total output increased 0.9 percent last month, the biggest monthly increase since a 1.3 percent jump last February, the Federal Reserve said.

"The Fed doesn't set policy decisions on one number but the fact that it's the day before the meeting has people nervous," said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist at Van Kampen American Capital.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was off 21/32, raising its yield, which moves in the opposite direction from the price, to 6.63 percent from 6.58 percent at Friday's close.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 7.65 to 720.99. The American Stock Exchange index lost 3.49 to 572.37.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 3.22 to 380.85. The average share was down 34 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 6,998.623 down 74.075 or 1.05 percent.
